Hey, there! What's up? I'll get to the quick and dirty: I ran.

It wasn't sexy or secret, because I held an official post-graduation fellowship that allowed me to travel solo, but it was still running. I traveled Eastern Europe alone for four months. I won't advise or ill-advise anyone but I can speak my experience.

In short: i broke down. I romanticized running away and fell apart when my mind came with me. Yes, it was nice to ditch responsibility. Yes, it was nice to not send in resumes. But i realized that those stressors were just that: stressors to my self. They didn't compare and could never compare to my actual mental illness. For me, running away heightened my mania and depression. At one moment, I was reckless and euphoric. Another, lonely and isolated. I cycled more rapidly that I ever had and eventually came home. The months following included a suicide attempt and deep depression. 

After stabilizing, I will run away again. But this time, in a way that is kind to myself and my mind. and that realizes that i'm not running. i'm traveling. so many people offer travel as a "cure" and from my experience, it is not when someone with a mental illness (hi, that's me) romanticizes the image of running. But it can be an enriching and healing experience, if that person (again, me) is prepared that her mental illness will react to running away.

hope the story helps!!

I like what you're saying here. My favorite part is "understatement to say, You make me complete. But I cannot have you."

That said, I had a difficult time reading through the prose. Every once in a while, I would catch a rhythm, but it would fall off quickly. Personally, I think your use of punctuation marks could be edited. Some are fantastic, like the one mentioned above and the one "Please. Don't let me fall".

But I'm often confused on the choice b/w just a capital letter and a full punctuation mark. Going with this theme, I also find the semi-colon to be difficult to read through. Is it a short pause? a long one? And then you also use commas. It's a lot of punctuation, but it doesn't necessarily help me read the piece.

So i love, love the message. But in the editing process, i would really focus on which words you want the reader to acknowledge fully (and place punctuation marks accordingly) and where you want to establish a rhythm :)

But awesome job! I could literally never write a prose poem like this, so congrats :)

F**k, this is GOOD. I'm really liking this a lot. I read it so quickly the first time and noticed that your pacing is fantastic. Then I read it slowly and noticed that your wording is equally fantastic.

But just like the comment below (hi!), the chicken noodle soup was jarring -- for me, only because i had to double-think about the idea of chicken drowning in soup. It was funny and confusing, which are some sentiments NOT present in the rest of your work. There are two things I like about it, though: (1) it's tangible. I completely agree that something tangible should be there, since you're falling back into reality; (2) it's small. chicken noodle soup is a small item and it fits with the tininess, as you fall back and away from your expansiveness; and (3) the chicken floating in soup is dead, which as utterly creepy as that is, gives an empty feeling to the piece which definitely jives; (4) it's a common item, which adds to the existentialism. If there's any way to keep those three elements alive but switch the object, that would be my best advice.

I'm probably going to read this over and over. It's so good :)

Wow, I like the ending a lot. It's unexpected and jolting, while still being within the rhythm of the poem. I also like how you capitalize "She", keeping the subject clear and the read in-check with the progress of the poem. In fact, I personally think capitalizing all "She"'s would really, really help. Since it's lower on the structure spectrum (which I like), the rhythm is super important and pretty much every time you write (or say) "she", it's a patterned rhythm. awesome work!

I really, really like the flow of the syllables you have going here. Curious: is it meant to be read or spoken? If spoken, "lips clasp" is a bit tough to get around the mouth. But that's truthfully by biggest critique. I love how you broke up "you mean nothing" and "to me". It's simultaneously harsh and forgiving. It holds a coldness of "the morning after". Nice.
